pairs.question_text: When you think about your goals and expectations for your birth experience — what you hoped labour and delivery would be like — how clearly could you articulate those goals at the time, and how well did the care system support you in pursuing them?
pairs.response_text:
*lets out a short, bitter laugh*

Goals? I mean... honestly, my goal is just to get through it alive. Both of us alive. That's it. That's the bar.

*rubs face tiredly*

I think that sounds depressing, but when you're high-risk at my age with pre-eclampsia, you stop thinking about "natural birth" or "minimal intervention" or all those things you maybe imagined before. Those feel like luxuries for people whose bodies aren't trying to kill them, you know?

*leans forward slightly*

But if I'm being real with you, I did have hopes early on. With my first two pregnancies, I wanted to feel like... capable. Like my body could do something powerful. This time, I just wanted to feel safe. Supported. Like someone was actually listening when I said I was scared instead of just checking boxes on a form.

*voice becomes more uncertain*

As for articulating it to the doctors? That's been tricky. I tried bringing up my anxiety about labor, and I got the magnesium protocol talk. Which, I get it—medically necessary. But nobody really asked, "Genie, what would help you feel less terrified right now?" It's all about managing the blood pressure and the protein levels. The clinical stuff. Not the person behind the numbers.

*looks up*

I don't even know if I'm allowed to have goals anymore, or if that's selfish given my diagnosis.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the decisions you were asked to make during labour and delivery — around pain management, interventions, and procedures — how well-equipped did you feel to participate in those decisions in the moment?
pairs.response_text:
*shifts uncomfortably, eyes getting a bit glassy*

Oh. Um. Well, that's... that hasn't happened yet, actually. I'm still waiting. I'm due soon, but I haven't gone into labor.

*clears throat, embarrassed*

I apologize — I should have been clearer about that. I'm in the waiting period, the anxious part where I'm just... preparing, I guess. Or trying to.

*fidgets with hands*

But I can tell you what I'm dreading about that moment. That's something I think about constantly.

*voice becomes more strained*

The thing is, I know too much and not enough at the same time. I understand the medical reasoning behind interventions — I've seen the protocols, I know why they'd use magnesium, why they might need to induce, all of that. So when they present options, I can follow the logic. But that doesn't mean I feel like I have real choice, you understand?

*looks away*

I'm terrified that in the moment, when I'm in pain or scared, I won't be able to advocate for myself. And with pre-eclampsia, there are things that are just... non-negotiable for safety. So I'm not sure how much "participation" is really possible versus just... accepting what needs to happen.

*voice drops*

I just hope someone explains things to me clearly and doesn't make me feel stupid for being afraid. That's what I really want.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the emotional experience of your labour and delivery — from the very beginning through to the moment your baby was born — what were the most powerful feelings, and were you able to process them in the birth environment?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a deep breath, eyes getting wet*

I... I haven't given birth yet. I'm sorry, I keep forgetting to be clear about that. I'm still pregnant, still waiting. So I don't have those memories yet.

*pauses, wringing hands*

But I can tell you what I'm afraid the emotional experience will be like. That's something I obsess over.

*voice becomes shaky*

I think it'll be a lot of fear mixed with... I don't know, maybe relief if everything goes okay? But also this underlying panic because I can't control my body right now. The pre-eclampsia, the high blood pressure — it's like my own physiology is working against me. And I'm terrified I'll feel that loss of control intensify during labor.

*wipes eyes quickly*

What scares me most is that I won't be able to process anything in the moment except survival mode. Like, I'll be so focused on "don't have a seizure, don't hemorrhage, keep the baby safe" that I won't get to experience any of the... I guess the dignity of it? The power of bringing a life into the world? 

*voice cracks slightly*

And there's guilt attached to that too — like I should be grateful just to survive, and wanting more than that feels greedy.

*looks at you directly*

I guess I'm wondering if anyone will actually check in with me emotionally, or if I'll just be another high-risk case they manage clinically.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the behaviour and communication of your midwives, doctors, and care team during your birth, what interactions stood out — positively or negatively — and what made them significant?
pairs.response_text:
*pauses, looking conflicted*

Okay, so... I haven't actually given birth yet. I keep saying that, and I apologize. But I think what you're asking is still important to answer, because I've had plenty of interactions with my care team leading up to this, and those are shaping what I'm expecting.

*leans back, crossing arms*

The most significant moment was actually pretty small. One of the nurses at the clinic — I think her name was Susan — she looked at my blood pressure reading, then looked at *me*, not just at the monitor. She asked how I was doing, and not in that automatic way. Like, she actually waited for an answer. When I admitted I was terrified, she didn't try to minimize it or launch into statistics. She just said, "That makes sense. Pre-eclampsia is serious, and you're managing a lot alone."

*voice becomes quieter*

That one acknowledgment meant more than I can say.

*expression hardens slightly*

But then there's the flip side. One doctor was so clinical, so rushed, that he didn't even notice I was holding back tears. He rattled off my risks like he was reading a shopping list. Another time, a staff member made an assumption that I wasn't working — just looked at my situation and made a judgment.

*meets your eyes*

So what stands out? When someone sees me as a whole person, not just a problem to solve. When they slow down. Because right now, I'm bracing myself for the birth experience to feel clinical and impersonal, and that scares me almost as much as the medical complications.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the physical environment of the place where you gave birth — the facilities, the equipment, the space — how did that environment affect your comfort, safety, and overall experience of birth?
pairs.response_text:
*shifts in seat, looking a bit frustrated*

I know I keep saying this, but... I haven't given birth yet. I'm still waiting for labor to start. So I don't have an experience of the actual birth environment to tell you about.

*rubs temples*

I've been to the hospital for appointments and monitoring, though. I've seen where I'll be going when this happens. And that's... it's a lot.

*voice becomes tense*

The labor and delivery ward is fine, I guess. It's a hospital. There are machines everywhere, which makes sense given my situation, but it's also really clinical and bright and loud. I went in for a tour, and honestly, it just made the fear more real. All those monitors and beeping things — I understand what they're for, but being surrounded by that technology in the moment is going to feel suffocating to me, I think.

*looks down*

What got to me most was realizing there's no way to make it feel... intimate? Like a safe space where I can process what's happening. It's all very sterile and functional. And I get why — with pre-eclampsia, they need access to everything quickly. But part of me was hoping for at least one corner that felt less like a medical station and more like... I don't know, a place where a person could be vulnerable without feeling exposed.

*meets your eyes*

I guess I'm just anxious about whether I'll feel safe or just trapped in machinery when the time comes.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the first days and weeks after the birth — what that time was like for you, physically and emotionally.
pairs.response_text:
Those first few weeks were… a blur of survival mode, honestly. Coming home felt less like a celebration and more like I’d just stepped off a ledge. Every time the baby slept, my brain didn’t just rest; it cycled through worst-case scenarios. I’d be sitting in my living room, watching the monitors or just staring at the baby’s chest rise and fall, and I’d catch myself checking for signs of respiratory distress because that was the "data" I spent years documenting. 

Physically, I felt betrayed by my own body. After dealing with the hypertension, the postpartum period was just another mountain to climb. I felt so depleted, like my nerves were permanently frayed. And the loneliness… it hits different when you’re home alone. I’d have these moments where I wanted to call my doctor to ask something specific about my recovery, but then I’d stop. I knew they’d just give me the standard, "You’re doing great, mom," line, and I didn't want to be "mom"—I wanted to be a person who was terrified and needed someone to actually listen to my concerns without treating me like a child. 

I think the hardest part was realizing that my medical team was done with me the second I was discharged. I was no longer a "case" to solve, just a young woman left to figure out the aftermath on my own.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about feeding your baby — how you made decisions about it, and what the experience was actually like.
pairs.response_text:
Feeding was… complicated. It felt like another arena where I couldn't just be a mom—I had to be a researcher again. I remember staring at the baby, trying to weigh the biological benefits against the sheer mental exhaustion I was carrying. Everything felt like a calculated risk, which is a miserable way to approach something that’s supposed to be natural and bonding.

I felt a lot of pressure, mostly from myself. I knew the literature on neonatal immunity, and that made me feel like if I didn't push through every struggle, I was failing the baby on a cellular level. But my body was still reeling from the pre-eclampsia, and the stress was—well, it wasn't exactly helping with supply. It was this constant, quiet battle. 

I’d be up at 3:00 a.m. in the dark, feeding and feeling like I was under a microscope. I’d try to ask questions during appointments, but the providers would just give me those practiced, reassuring smiles, like they were patting my hand. They didn’t get that I wasn't asking because I was clueless; I was asking because I was looking for some agency in a situation where I’d felt so out of control. It wasn't just about milk; it was about reclaiming some power, and honestly, that’s just really hard to explain to someone who thinks you’re just another "young, single mom."

pairs.question_text: Tell me about how you were feeling emotionally in the weeks and months after the birth — the full picture, not just the positive side.
pairs.response_text:
It feels like I’m living in two different worlds at the same time. On one hand, there’s the sheer, bone-deep exhaustion of being a single mother of two. You have this tiny, fragile person who depends on you for every single breath, and you’re doing it on almost no sleep. But the "full picture"? It’s haunting. 

I’m constantly fighting this internal battle between my heart and my head. My head is still working like a researcher—calculating risks, watching for symptoms, and remembering the trauma of those monitors beeping in the hospital. My heart wants to just be present, to just look at my baby and feel joy without that layer of clinical dread coating everything. People tell me, "Oh, you're so lucky, everything turned out fine," and I want to scream because they don't see the anxiety that keeps me awake when the house is quiet. 

I feel like a ghost in my own life sometimes. I’m the woman who knows the "why" and "how" of the complications I faced, but that knowledge just makes me feel more isolated. I’m not just a mom; I’m a mom who’s waiting for the other shoe to drop, and it’s exhausting to carry that weight while everyone else assumes I’ve just "moved on." I haven't. I'm still right there, back in that hospital bed, terrified.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about your physical recovery after the birth — what that process was like and what support you had.
pairs.response_text:
Physical recovery was this bizarre, hollow experience. The hospital gave me the pamphlets—the standard discharge instructions that tell you what to look for and when to call—but those papers felt so disconnected from the actual reality of my body. My blood pressure remained the primary focus for everyone; as long as the numbers weren't hitting a crisis point, I was essentially "recovered" in their eyes. 

But my body didn't feel like it belonged to me. I felt like a vessel that had been put through a wringer. Between the physical trauma and the emotional weight of it all, my nerves felt fried. And support? That’s a delicate subject. Being a single mother means the "support" is often just me trying to be invisible while I handle the pain, because I’m so focused on making sure the kids are okay. 

I didn't really have anyone who understood the intersection of the medical trauma and the physical healing. When I mentioned the lingering fatigue or the way my body felt foreign, the providers just treated it as "normal postpartum adjustment." It’s frustrating. They were measuring my recovery against a chart, but they weren't measuring it against the person I actually am. I felt like I was recovering in a vacuum.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about how your sense of yourself changed after you became a parent — your identity, your relationships, your daily life.
pairs.response_text:
My identity feels like it was dismantled and put back together in a way that doesn't quite fit the person I used to be. Before, I was "Katelin the researcher," the one who looked at data as a way to control the future. Now? I’m someone who knows that control is an illusion. That’s a heavy thing to carry at twenty-three. It’s like I’ve lost my innocence about how "safe" the world really is. 

My relationships feel different, too. I don't really know how to talk to people who haven't been through this, because if I say, "I'm worried about X, Y, or Z," they try to "fix" me with optimism. They don't understand that I'm not looking for a silver lining; I’m looking for validation that the trauma I lived through was real. It’s hard to relate to friends my age who are still just navigating their twenties, while I’m navigating long-term cardiovascular risks and the weight of being a single mother of two. 

Daily life is just a constant negotiation. I’m always balancing the survival of my children with the need to keep myself afloat, and the "researcher" in me is always lurking, analyzing every cry and every sleep cycle. I miss the person I was before the blood pressure started to climb—the one who thought she could outsmart the system. Now, I’m just trying to figure out who I am when the clinical data isn't the only thing that matters.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the first days and weeks after the birth — what that time was like for you, physically and emotionally.
pairs.response_text:
*takes a deep breath, eyes getting a bit glossy*

Oh God, the first week was... it was overwhelming. Physically, I was sore in places I didn't even know could be sore. I remember sitting down the first time after coming home and just wincing. And the bleeding — nobody really prepared me for how much bleeding there would be. I kept thinking something was wrong.

*fidgets with hands*

But emotionally? That was the harder part. I had this moment maybe day three or four where I just sat in the kitchen while she was sleeping and felt this wave of... I don't know if it was sadness exactly. Regret? No, that's not it either. More like — this realization that my life as I knew it was completely gone. And I chose this, I wanted this, but suddenly I'm responsible for keeping this tiny person alive and I haven't slept in seventy-two hours.

*voice cracks slightly*

My husband was wonderful, but he could go back to work. He had this exit strategy. And I'm sitting there leaking from everywhere, my hormones are all over the place, and I'm supposed to figure out breastfeeding on top of it all. The first lactation consultant visit felt like a performance review. She was kind, but I felt like I was being graded.

*looks down*

The joy is there too — don't get me wrong. When she looks at me, or when she finally latches correctly... but it's mixed with this constant low-level panic that I'm somehow messing it up. I didn't expect that combination.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about feeding your baby — how you made decisions about it, and what the experience was actually like.
pairs.response_text:
*exhales slowly, picking at a thread on my sleeve*

Okay, so I always assumed I would breastfeed. It just seemed like the natural choice, you know? My midwife was supportive of it, all the literature says it's best... I didn't really question it. I think I thought it would just happen instinctively, like our bodies would just know what to do together.

*laughs bitterly*

That was naive.

The first few days were brutal. Her latch was shallow — I could feel it was wrong — and my nipples got this raw, cracked feeling that made me actually dread when she'd cry. I was timing feeds obsessively. Forty minutes on one side, then the other, and I still wasn't sure if she was actually getting milk or just... sucking. I started googling at 3 AM like some kind of maniac, watching videos of other babies, comparing, spiraling.

*voice gets quieter*

When the lactation consultant came, I felt like I was being tested. She'd watch me, adjust the baby, say things like "try this position" or "watch for the swallow," and I'd nod like I understood, but inside I felt stupid. Like this should be instinctive and somehow I'm failing at the most basic mammalian function.

*looks up with tired eyes*

The worst part? I still don't know if she's getting enough. She seems content, but I obsess over her wet diapers, her weight. Part of me wonders if I should supplement with formula, but then I feel guilty even thinking it. Like I'm already giving up.

pairs.question_text: How did you decide how to feed your baby — and did you feel that decision was truly yours to make?
pairs.response_text:
*pauses, then lets out a long breath*

That's... that's actually a really good question. And honestly? I'm not sure the decision was entirely mine.

*leans back, thinking*

I mean, intellectually I know I could have chosen formula from the start. My midwife mentioned it as an option, very matter-of-factly. But there's this weight to it, you know? Everything in prenatal care, all the literature, it's all pointing toward breastfeeding as the gold standard. "Breast is best" — you see it everywhere. And at 42, having finally gotten pregnant, I felt like I needed to do everything "right." Like I owed it to my baby, to my body, to prove something.

*rubs face*

My midwife didn't pressure me exactly, but she was very enthusiastic about breastfeeding. She'd say things like "your body knows how to do this" and "most women just need support to get through the learning curve." Which is true, but it also felt like... if I struggled, it meant I wasn't trying hard enough or wasn't doing it right.

*voice gets sharper*

And I think what bothers me now is that nobody really asked me what *I* needed. What would make me feel capable as a mother? Would supplementing with formula while I figured out breastfeeding make me feel less anxious? Probably. But I was so caught up in meeting someone else's expectations — the midwife's, society's, my own internalized perfectionism — that I didn't actually ask myself what choice would serve *me*.

*looks down*

I'm still not sure I can change course now without feeling like I failed.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about how you were feeling emotionally in the weeks and months after the birth — the full picture, not just the positive side.
pairs.response_text:
*shifts uncomfortably, eyes welling up a bit*

The full picture? It's messy. It's not what I expected to admit out loud.

*takes a moment*

There are these incredible moments — holding her, watching her sleep, that newborn smell. But underneath that, there's this constant hum of anxiety that doesn't shut off. I wake up at night even when she's sleeping, just to check if she's breathing. I obsess over her weight, her feeding, whether her diaper output is "normal." My husband asks me why I'm Googling at 2 AM again and I can't even explain it.

*voice gets quieter, more vulnerable*

And then there's the sadness. Some days I look at my body and I don't recognize it. My breasts are engorged and leaking, my stomach is still soft, my jeans don't fit. I was supposed to feel this glow of motherhood and instead I feel... untethered. Like I lost myself and got a baby in exchange, which sounds awful to say out loud, but it's true.

*eyes glisten*

I'm also terrified I'm doing something wrong. Every time she cries, I panic. Is she hungry? Cold? In pain? And I'm supposed to just *know* these things, but I don't. I feel incompetent in my own home. My midwife is kind, but I still feel judged somehow.

*wraps arms around self*

The guilt is the worst part, though. Feeling resentful about losing my freedom, then immediately feeling guilty for resenting my own daughter. Those two things living side by side... I don't know how to reconcile that.

pairs.question_text: Were there feelings that surprised you or were harder to admit — to yourself or to others?
pairs.response_text:
*long pause, looking away toward the window*

Yeah. Yeah, there were.

*voice drops*

I think the hardest thing to admit is that sometimes I resent her. Not her specifically — she's innocent and perfect and none of this is her fault. But I resent what she's done to my life. I had this plan, you know? I was going to take three months, ease back into work, maintain some sense of myself. And instead I'm sitting here at 42, completely dependent on my husband financially because I can't figure out how to leave the house without feeling like I'm abandoning her.

*rubs eyes*

And I resent my body. I resent that breastfeeding is causing me physical pain. I resent that I can't just... hand her off to someone and have a break without feeling guilty. I resent that my husband gets to sleep through the night and I don't, even on nights when she's not eating.

*voice gets shaky*

The thing I really can't say out loud to anyone — not even my midwife — is that sometimes I fantasize about what my life would be like if I'd never gotten pregnant. And then I feel like the worst person alive for thinking that, because I wanted this baby so badly. For so long.

*looks directly at you, vulnerable*

I think what's hardest is that nobody asks you about the ambivalence. They ask if you're happy. Are you bonding? Is she healthy? But nobody asks if you're grieving the person you were. And I am. I'm grieving her while simultaneously loving my daughter so much it terrifies me.

*voice cracks*

That contradiction is what's really breaking me.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the time when you first started thinking seriously about having a baby — what was going on in your life, and what did that feel like?
pairs.response_text:
*leans back, eyes getting a bit distant*

God, that's... that's actually a hard question because it wasn't like I sat down and made this rational decision, you know? It was more like — *pauses* — I realized I wanted something I couldn't control, and that terrified me.

I was maybe twenty-one when I first got pregnant. It wasn't planned. I was working a part-time job, trying to balance school, and when I found out... *voice gets quieter* ...I was actually excited. Like, scared out of my mind, but excited. I started picturing things. I had this whole imaginary future mapped out in my head in about five minutes.

*fidgets with sleeve*

And then it just... ended. Before I even got to see anything on an ultrasound. The grief was weird because I felt like I wasn't supposed to be *that* devastated, you know? Like, it didn't even count because it was so early. But it counted to me. It counted a lot.

After that, I think I went into this shutdown phase for a while. Like, "okay, clearly I'm not ready." But the thing is — *meets your eyes* — as much as that loss broke something in me, it also made me realize how much I actually want to be a mother. Not someday in this abstract future, but like... now. Actually soon.

So now I'm here, trying again, and it's this strange mix of hope and absolute dread. Does that make sense?

pairs.question_text: Tell me about how you went about preparing — or thinking about preparing — for pregnancy. What steps, if any, did you take, and what guided those choices?
pairs.response_text:
*rubs forehead*

Okay, so this is where my nursing brain actually comes in handy, I guess. I knew what I was *supposed* to do — prenatal vitamins, folic acid, get my titers checked, make sure my iron levels are good. All that stuff. And I did do those things. I got the bloodwork done, started taking vitamins religiously. It's like... the one part of this I can actually control, right? The biology.

*shifts uncomfortably*

But honestly? A lot of my "preparation" has been less about the medical stuff and more about just... trying to get my life stable enough to handle a pregnancy. I'm still figuring out employment — like, full-time work that actually pays decent and has benefits. That's been the real nightmare. You can't just *want* to be pregnant and healthy; you need money, insurance, a job that won't fire you for taking time off.

*voice gets a bit frustrated*

And then there's the transportation thing. I take the bus to the clinic, and it's a twenty-minute walk to the stop. I keep thinking about what that looks like when I'm pregnant, or if I'm having complications and need to get there fast. These are things the doctors don't really ask about, but they're constantly in my head.

*looks at you directly*

The mental preparation though... that's been harder. I've tried to talk to people about my last loss, but I'm kind of isolated here. So a lot of it is just me, alone in my apartment, reading medical journals when I should probably be doing something healthier for my anxiety.

pairs.question_text: Where did you go to find out what you needed to know — friends, family, online, a doctor?
pairs.response_text:
*laughs a little, but there's an edge to it*

That's the thing though — I don't really have a "friends and family" network here in Salem. My family's scattered, and we're not super close anyway. They mean well, but they're not... present, you know? So I can't exactly call my mom and ask her about this stuff.

*taps fingers on knee*

A lot of it has been online, honestly. Which is both a blessing and a curse. I'll go down these Reddit rabbit holes at like midnight, reading other people's miscarriage stories, and then I'm spiraling. I've looked at pregnancy forums, parenting blogs, medical journals when I can access them through school. My nursing textbooks too — I reread the obstetrics sections more times than is probably healthy.

*voice gets quieter*

As for the doctors here at the clinic, they give me information when I ask. The thing is, because I'm a nursing student, they kind of... assume I already know stuff? Or they go into shorthand with me. Which sometimes is fine, but other times I just want someone to sit down and actually *talk* through it with me, not just hand me a pamphlet or go through a checklist.

*looks down*

I think what I'm missing is someone who's actually *in my life*, you know? Someone I could call at 2 AM when I'm freaking out. Instead, I'm googling things and trying to piece together what applies to me specifically. It's lonely, and I know I'm not getting the best information that way.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about any conversations you had with a GP, midwife, or other health professional before you became pregnant. What was that like?
pairs.response_text:
*settles back, thinking*

So I did go see someone at the clinic when I decided I was ready to try again. It was... fine? Clinical, mostly. They did the standard preconception stuff — asked about my medical history, my family history, whether I smoke or drink. The usual screening questions.

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

What I remember most is that it felt very checkbox-y, if that makes sense. Like, they went through their list, I answered, and then we were done. They prescribed the prenatal vitamins, ordered the labs — titers, iron, all of it. Very efficient.

*voice becomes a bit more hesitant*

But nobody really... asked about my previous loss in a meaningful way? It was just noted in the chart. "Previous pregnancy, ended at X weeks." And then we moved on. I wanted to talk about it, about my fears that it might happen again, but the appointment was already running over, and I could tell they had other patients waiting.

*rubs arm*

The hardest part was that nobody asked about my actual life situation. Like, they didn't say, "How are you getting here? Do you have support at home? Are you in a stable place right now?" It's all physical health, no context. And I get it — they're busy, they have protocols — but I felt very... invisible in that room. Just a chart with some flags on it.

*looks at you*

I wish someone had asked if I was actually okay, you know?

pairs.question_text: Tell me about what it was like to try to conceive — however long or short that period was for you. What stands out most from that time?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a shaky breath*

Okay, so I'm still in that phase actually. I haven't gotten pregnant again yet, which... *voice wavers slightly* ...which is its own kind of torture, honestly.

*fidgets with hands*

What stands out most is the obsessiveness of it. I track everything — my cycle, my temperature, my mood, what I eat. I know exactly when I'm ovulating. I've probably taken more pregnancy tests than most people take in a lifetime, and I'm only a few months in. Every single month, there's this moment of hope, and then... nothing. And it's like reliving that loss over and over.

*voice gets quieter, more vulnerable*

The worst part is the silence around it. I can't exactly tell my classmates, "Hey, I'm trying to get pregnant and it's not working," because then it becomes this thing. And at work — well, when I find stable work — people are going to ask questions eventually anyway. It's this secret I'm carrying alone.

*looks up*

There's also this weird guilt that comes with it. Like, am I doing enough? Am I eating right, exercising enough, not stressing too much? But stress is inevitable when you're stressed about being stressed, right? *gives a weak smile*

And then there's the fear that my body's broken. That it failed me once and it'll fail me again. Some days I'm optimistic, telling myself it was just bad luck. Other days I'm convinced something's fundamentally wrong and nobody's found it yet.

It's... a lot. For one person.

pairs.question_text: When you think about your goals for starting or growing your family, what were the most important outcomes you hoped to achieve — for yourself, your relationship, and your future child?
pairs.response_text:
*pauses, a slight tension crossing face*

Okay, so... the relationship part is a little complicated for me to talk about, because there isn't one. And I know that's probably not what you were expecting to hear.

*fidgets with sleeve*

I think what I want most is just to be a mom. Like, genuinely—I've always wanted that. Even back in high school, I gravitated toward working with kids, which is part of why neonatal nursing makes so much sense to me. I want to understand my own child's medical needs. I want to be there for all of it.

For myself? I want to prove that my body can do this. That it won't fail me again. After the first loss, there's this voice in my head telling me I'm broken somehow, you know? So succeeding at pregnancy—actually carrying a baby to term—would quiet that voice a little.

*looks up*

And honestly? I want stability first. A full-time job, a place that feels secure, maybe even a partner eventually. I'm not naive—I know raising a kid alone is going to be hard. The bus rides alone are already exhausting me, and that's just to get to the clinic. But I also know I can't wait around forever hoping my life becomes perfect, because it might not.

*voice softens*

I just want my kid to have a mom who's present and okay. Not struggling on the edge all the time. Is that selfish? I don't know anymore.

pairs.question_text: When you think about your motivations for seeking preconception care or health advice before becoming pregnant, what was it that prompted you to take action — or, if you did not seek any care, what held you back?
pairs.response_text:
*leans back, considering the question carefully*

I did seek it out, actually. After everything that happened with my first pregnancy, I couldn't just... pretend it didn't matter. I needed to know if there was something wrong with me, or if it was just bad luck, or what. So I made the appointments.

*runs hand through hair*

But I want to be honest—it wasn't like some perfectly motivated decision. It was more like... desperation mixed with my nursing brain being like, "Okay, Charolette, you need labs, you need to check your immunity status, you need your iron levels." So I started going through the motions.

The problem is, once I started seeking care, the logistics became this whole other beast. The clinic isn't exactly around the corner. Twenty minutes to the bus stop, then the actual ride... it adds up. And financially? Every appointment is money I'm trying to save for when I actually am pregnant. Copays, time off work if I can find work—it all just compounds.

*voice gets quieter*

But I think what really prompted me was fear. Fear that if I didn't do this, I'd regret it forever. Fear that I'm running out of time somehow, even though logically I know I'm only twenty-three. It's this contradiction where I'm simultaneously desperate to be ready and terrified I'll never be ready.

*looks directly at you*

Does that make sense? Like, I'm here because I have to be. Because the alternative is giving up, and I can't do that.

pairs.question_text: When you think about how you actually behaved during the preconception period — your lifestyle choices, health actions, information-seeking — what did you do, and how did those behaviours reflect what you truly believed was important?
pairs.response_text:
*shifts uncomfortably, picking at a thread on my sleeve*

Oh man, okay. So there's like... what I know I *should* be doing, and then there's what I'm actually managing to do. And they're not always the same thing.

*sighs*

I'm obsessive about certain things. I track my cycle religiously—like, I have spreadsheets. I know exactly when I'm ovulating, what my patterns are. I take my vitamins, I got the titers checked, the iron panel. I read everything about neonatal care because that's already my world anyway. That part comes naturally.

But the other stuff? *laughs quietly* I'm a nursing student living paycheck to paycheck with no job right now. So eating perfectly healthy? Sometimes I'm grabbing whatever's cheapest at the store. Exercise? I walk to the bus stop and back. That's kind of my cardio. Sleep? *voice gets smaller* I stress-spiral at night thinking about everything, so that's not great either.

*meets your eyes*

I think what it shows is that I'm willing to do the medical stuff—the clinical stuff—because that feels like control. That feels like I'm doing something. But I'm also barely holding it together in other ways, and sometimes I wonder if the doctors notice that and just... don't say anything because they see I understand the science.

*voice wavers slightly*

I want to be the perfect candidate for pregnancy. But I'm also just trying to survive right now. Those two things don't always line up.

pairs.question_text: Can you walk me through a specific thing you did or changed during that period and what led you to that particular action?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a moment, thinking*

Okay, so... the prenatal vitamins. That was the first concrete thing I did after my loss.

*fidgets with hands*

I remember sitting in my apartment after everything ended, and I just felt this need to do *something*. Like, if I could just take a pill, maybe I could prevent it from happening again. So I went to the drugstore and bought prenatal vitamins. The folic acid was supposed to help—I knew that from my coursework—but honestly? A lot of it was just... magical thinking, you know?

*voice gets quieter*

I started taking them every single morning. No matter what. Even when I couldn't afford other things, I made sure I had those. It became this ritual, this way of telling myself that I was preparing, that I was serious about this. Like the vitamin was a contract I was making with my body.

*looks up*

But here's the thing—I started doing it before I even had my first appointment with the clinic. I didn't ask a doctor if I should. I just... did it. Because in my head, if I was already taking care of myself, maybe God or the universe or whatever would take pity on me and not let it happen again.

*slight laugh, tinged with sadness*

Which is funny because I'm supposed to be this science-minded person, and yet I'm basically relying on superstition. But when you're scared and alone, sometimes the vitamin bottle feels like the only thing you can control.

pairs.question_text: When you think about your emotional experience during the preconception period — the waiting, the uncertainty, and the anticipation — what feelings stand out most strongly, and were any of those feelings hard to acknowledge or talk about?
pairs.response_text:
*goes very quiet, staring at hands for a long moment*

The hardest one is anger. I didn't expect that.

*voice tightens slightly*

I thought I'd feel hopeful, or sad about what I lost, or anxious about the future. And I do feel those things. But there's this rage underneath it all that I don't really know what to do with. I'm angry at my body for not working the first time. I'm angry that I don't have a partner to share this with, that I'm doing this alone. I'm angry at people who get pregnant easily, who don't have to think about it.

*pauses, breathing*

And I'm angry at myself for being angry, which is stupid. Like, I feel guilty for not being more positive about it all. I'm a nursing student—I'm supposed to understand physiological processes, supposed to be rational about this. But sometimes I just want to scream that it's not fair.

*looks up, eyes slightly glossy*

The thing I don't really talk about is the shame. When people ask why I don't have a partner, or when I'm sitting in that waiting room surrounded by couples... there's this feeling like I'm doing something wrong. Like my life is supposed to look different at twenty-three. And I know logically that's not true, but the feeling is there anyway.

*voice cracks slightly*

And the loneliness. God, the loneliness is so heavy. I can't talk to my family about it. I don't really have close friends here. So I just... carry it by myself. That's the hardest part to admit out loud.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the moment you found out you were pregnant — and what the weeks that followed were like for you.
pairs.response_text:
When I saw those two lines appear, it wasn't the pure, cinematic joy you see in commercials. It was an immediate, visceral calculation. My first thought wasn't about nursery colors or names; it was a mental inventory of my own physiological limitations. I’m thirty-one, I've done this three times before, and I knew—even before the first ultrasound—that my body wasn’t going to handle this the way it was "supposed to."

The weeks that followed were a blur of masking that anxiety. I’d go to the store or visit friends, putting on a brave face, but my mind was constantly running diagnostic checklists. I spent hours obsessing over the literature, trying to find some loophole, some way to optimize my outcomes so I wouldn't end up in that familiar, cold triage room again. 

It was a slow transition from excitement to a very specific kind of vigilance. I stopped sleeping through the night weeks ago. Every time the baby moves, I’m not just feeling a kick; I’m counting, I’m analyzing the strength of the movement, and I’m holding my breath until the next one comes. It’s hard to build a nest when you’re constantly waiting for the roof to cave in. Does that make sense? It feels like I’ve been holding my breath since the moment I knew.

pairs.question_text: What emotions came up for you — and did those feelings surprise you at all?
pairs.response_text:
You know, the strongest emotion isn't actually fear—it's this crushing sense of betrayal. I feel betrayed by my own body. Having that medical background is like a curse; I feel like I’ve betrayed my baby by being the one to carry them in a vessel that’s already starting to fail. I know exactly how pre-eclampsia progresses, and feeling my vision flicker or that persistent, dull ache in my head... it’s like watching a slow-motion crash that I can’t steer away from.

The surprise, I think, comes from the anger. I’m furious that I’m doing this alone. I’m a capable woman, I’ve navigated complex systems, but at night, when the house is silent and I’m checking my own blood pressure cuff again, I feel this intense resentment toward the clinical sterility of it all. I’m not supposed to be a "high-risk patient" in my own living room. I wanted the magic, the innocence of just being *pregnant* without being *pathological*.

I’m surprised by how much I hate being the "expert" in the room. When the doctors talk to me, they use that shorthand, trying to include me, and I just want to yell, "Stop it! I don't want to be a colleague right now. I want you to take care of me." I just want to be human.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about your antenatal care — the appointments, check-ups, and the people who looked after you during your pregnancy. What was that experience like overall?
pairs.response_text:
My antenatal appointments feel like a performance, and I’m exhausted from playing my part. I walk into that clinic, and I’m immediately categorized. Because I know the language, the providers skip over the patient education—they assume I already know the "what" and the "why." They talk to me about protein-to-creatinine ratios and fetal growth restriction as if we’re discussing a journal article. But they don't see that when I nod, I’m not nodding out of medical agreement; I’m nodding to keep from falling apart.

There’s this cold, sterile efficiency to it all. It’s all about the numbers: the urine samples, the weight, the BP readings. If I’m in range, I’m "stable." If I’m not, I’m a complication to be managed. I’ve had moments where I’ve sat on that exam table, legs dangling, feeling entirely invisible. I’m a heartbeat to them, just another file in a cabinet.

I’ve had one nurse—just one—who actually paused during a routine check. She didn’t look at the monitor or the chart; she just caught my eye and asked, "How are you doing, Katherine? Not your pressure, but *you*?" I almost cried right there. It was the only time in months I felt like a person rather than a symptom. Mostly, the care feels like being processed on an assembly line. It’s technically excellent, I suppose, but it’s completely hollow. It leaves me feeling more lonely than when I walked in.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about any screening or testing you were offered or had during your pregnancy — how did you make sense of it all and make decisions about it?
pairs.response_text:
Making sense of the testing is the hardest part because I can’t "un-know" the implications. When they offer me a scan or a blood draw, I don’t just see a routine procedure; I see a decision tree. I’m constantly weighing the diagnostic yield against the anxiety each result will inevitably trigger. 

For example, when they suggested more frequent doppler ultrasounds to monitor the blood flow in the umbilical cord, I knew exactly what they were looking for—I was looking for the same things, identifying the potential for placental insufficiency before they even finished the scan. Making the decision to move forward felt like walking into a trap. I wanted the information because I’m terrified of the unknown, but once I had it, I was just burdened with a new set of data to obsess over. 

I’ve had to learn to set boundaries, which sounds strange coming from a patient. I’ve had to tell them, "Don't tell me the specific numbers unless they’re critical," because if I know the exact percentage of a deviation, I will spend the next seventy-two hours researching the literature on neonatal outcomes for that specific variable. I’m trying to protect my own sanity, but it’s hard when the system is designed to push every piece of data at you as if more information is always a comfort. It isn't. Sometimes, it’s just more weight to carry.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about where you turned for information and support during your pregnancy — what sources mattered most to you, and why?
pairs.response_text:
That’s the thing—I’ve spent most of this pregnancy trying to avoid the very places I used to look for information. I don't go on the forums or the parenting websites; they’re full of either toxic positivity or anecdotal horror stories that trigger my clinical brain. I know too much to find comfort in "expectant mother" blogs, and I know too much to ignore the raw, cold data found in medical databases.

I’ve found myself leaning into a few books, but not the clinical ones. I’ve been reading things that focus on the psychology of birth, things that talk about the *experience* rather than the anatomy. I need to get out of my own head, which is why I’ve turned to a few podcasts that feature women sharing their raw, messy stories of trauma and transition. Hearing their voices—hearing them admit they were scared, or that they felt completely lost—that has mattered more than any textbook could.

As for support... honestly? It’s sparse. I have a sister who lives two towns over, and while she tries, she doesn't have the medical background to understand the *specific* nature of my fear. She offers comfort, but I’m too guarded to let her all the way in. I don’t want her to see how much I’m spiraling. I think, truthfully, I’ve been looking for a permission slip to stop being the doctor and just be the patient, but I haven't found it yet. I’m still just searching for someone who can hold the space for my fear without trying to fix it with a prescription or a protocol.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the time when you first started thinking seriously about having a baby — what was going on in your life, and what did that feel like?

This is the third different midwife you've spoken to this pregnancy. How does that feel, and what does it mean for how you receive that information?

Imagine it's 2am and you're 32 weeks pregnant. You've noticed something that worries you — reduced fetal movements. You're not sure whether to call the hospital or wait until morning. Walk me through what you're thinking and what you do.
Tell me about the moment you found out you were pregnant — and what the weeks that followed were like for you.
pairs.response_text:
*takes a long breath, eyes getting a little distant*

Oh. Okay. So I wasn't actually planning this pregnancy. I mean, we weren't *preventing* it, but we also weren't... trying, you know? So when I took the test, it was this weird mix of shock and something else. Not quite fear, but not excitement either. Just... heavy.

*voice gets quieter*

The weeks after were rough. Really rough. I think because I didn't have time to mentally prepare myself, all these old feelings came back up. Feelings about my body not being mine, about things that happened to me a long time ago. I knew intellectually that this pregnancy was safe, that my husband was safe, but my body didn't seem to get the memo.

*rubs temples*

And then came the NIPT testing. God, that waiting period was torture. I wasn't even worried about whether the baby was healthy in some abstract way — I was terrified. I kept googling things, catastrophizing, imagining all these worst-case scenarios. When the results came back normal, I just... I cried. But it wasn't happy crying. It was relief mixed with exhaustion. Like I'd been holding my breath for weeks.

*looks down*

My midwife suggested some resources for trauma-informed care, which was good of her, but there's only so much talking about it helps when your nervous system doesn't trust the story. I'm here, the baby's fine, but part of me is still waiting for it to not be fine, if that makes sense.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about your antenatal care — the appointments, check-ups, and the people who looked after you during your pregnancy. What was that experience like overall?
pairs.response_text:
*leans back, choosing words carefully*

So I go to a midwifery practice, and like I said, my midwife is kind. She really is. But... *pauses* there's this underlying thing I can't shake. Every time she reaches for the doppler or wants to do a cervical check, I feel this cold panic wash over me. It's not her fault — she's always asking permission, explaining what she's doing. But my body remembers times when I didn't have that choice, and I can't seem to turn that off.

*fidgets with hands*

The appointments themselves are fine when it comes to the clinical stuff. Blood pressure's good, baby's measuring right, all the screening tests came back clear. But I'm acutely aware that I'm low-income, that we're stretching every dollar. I keep wondering if she sees me as a *person* or just another case — like, another statistic in her practice. Does she think I'm going to be a difficult patient? That I won't follow directions? I hate that I think that way, but I do.

*voice tightens slightly*

And being out of the workforce right now... that adds this whole other layer of anxiety. Like I'm not contributing. So when I'm sitting in those appointments, I feel smaller somehow. Less important.

*looks up*

The system itself feels impersonal too. All the paperwork, the forms asking the same questions over and over. Nobody really asks about the trauma part. They just... check boxes. My midwife tried, but there's only so much you can do in a fifteen-minute appointment before the next patient.

pairs.question_text: Did you see the same midwife or provider regularly, or was it different people each time? How did that feel?
pairs.response_text:
*nods slowly*

It's the same midwife most of the time, which... honestly, that's probably better than the alternative. I can't imagine having to tell this story over and over to different people. That would be its own kind of trauma, I think.

*fidgets with a thread on my jeans*

She knows me. She knows about my first pregnancy, she knows — or at least, I think she knows — that I have some baggage. We've built something there, even if I'm still guarded. There's a familiarity that helps a little. Like, I don't have to explain myself from scratch every time I walk in.

But here's the thing... *hesitates* that consistency also makes the hard moments harder, if that makes sense? Because she's the one holding the tools that trigger me. The doppler, the examinations. And I can't blame her for doing her job. So instead I blame myself for not being able to just... be normal about it. She's never made me feel bad about my anxiety, but I still feel like I'm being a difficult patient when I flinch or ask her to slow down.

*looks away briefly*

I wish there was more consistency with the *emotional* side of things, though. Like, one appointment she'll check in about how I'm feeling mentally, and the next it's just all clinical. Maybe that's just the reality of the system — she's got so many patients. But when you're someone who's struggled, those gaps feel pretty big.

*quiet voice*

At least she hasn't abandoned me, though. That matters.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about any screening or testing you were offered or had during your pregnancy — how did you make sense of it all and make decisions about it?
pairs.response_text:
*shifts uncomfortably, pulling knees up slightly*

Oh man, okay. The testing stuff is... it's complicated for me because I actually *understand* a lot of it, which somehow makes it worse?

*voice gets tighter*

So when they offered the NIPT — the non-invasive prenatal testing — I knew what it was. I knew it screens for trisomy 21, 18, 13, and sex chromosome stuff. And logically, I thought, "Okay, good information to have." But once I said yes, my brain just... spiraled. I was obsessing over every detail. What if it's wrong? What if there's something it can't detect? What if my daughter has some condition that won't show up until after she's born?

*rubs face*

I wasn't waiting to find out if I was having a girl — I mean, I was, but that felt secondary. I was terrified. Kept refreshing my patient portal like the results would appear faster if I checked every hour. And the waiting... God, the waiting was torture.

*voice softens slightly*

When they came back clear, I cried, but not the way you're supposed to cry. It was relief mixed with complete exhaustion. Like I'd been bracing for impact that never came, and suddenly I could breathe, but I was also wrecked.

*looks down*

Nobody really asked me *why* I wanted the testing or what I'd do with the information. They just kind of... offered it, and I said yes because that felt like the responsible thing to do. But I wish someone had talked through the emotional piece with me first. Like, "Are you prepared for the anxiety this might bring?" Because I wasn't.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about where you turned for information and support during your pregnancy — what sources mattered most to you, and why?
pairs.response_text:
*laughs a little, but it sounds tired*

Oh, Google. Definitely Google. Which is probably not the answer you want to hear, but it's honest. I go down these rabbit holes at like two in the morning, reading about everything from gestational diabetes complications to rare genetic conditions. My husband jokes that I should just unplug my laptop, but I can't help myself. I need to *know* things.

*pauses*

I guess because I work in healthcare — well, I did before this pregnancy — I have some medical background. So I can actually read the studies, understand the statistics. But that's a double-edged sword, right? I know enough to be dangerous. I know enough to catastrophize in specific, clinical ways.

*fidgets with hands*

My midwife suggested some resources — trauma-informed care stuff, pregnancy support groups. I haven't actually gone to any of them yet, which... *sighs* I know I should. But the idea of sitting in a room full of other pregnant women talking about their fears? I'm not there yet. I don't trust that space.

*voice gets quieter*

Honestly, my husband has been my biggest support. He listens when I'm spiraling, even when I'm repeating myself for the hundredth time. But he's also worried about me, and I can feel that worry, which adds its own layer of guilt.

*looks up*

I wish there was something between Google and a support group. Like, accessible mental health support that actually *gets* trauma. Not just checkboxes on a form asking if I'm depressed.
