pairs.response_text:
*leans back against the pillows, thinking*

Oh man, that's... yeah. I had *very* specific goals, actually. Maybe too specific? I spent weeks thinking about this.

The main thing was that quiet environment during the golden hour — I wanted her to have that calm introduction to the world, you know? Not bombarded with loud beeping machines and bright lights right when her sensory system is most vulnerable. I also wanted minimal intervention if possible, which... *laughs a little nervously* ...is ironic because I'm terrified of complications, but I also didn't want unnecessary stuff happening just because.

And I wanted skin-to-skin contact immediately. I read all the research on bonding and thermoregulation, and I just... I needed that.

*fidgets with the blanket*

When I came in and talked to the midwife about this stuff, she actually listened. Like, really listened. She didn't treat me like I was being precious or difficult. I think she understood that I had reasons behind what I was asking for, even if I didn't spell out that I'm basically a nerd who studies this stuff professionally.

But here's the thing — *voice gets more uncertain* — articulating goals is one thing. Sticking to them when you're in active labor? That's different. I keep second-guessing myself. Like, what if I need the epidural? What if my goals become impossible? The care system is supportive, but I'm realizing my goals are kind of... rigid. And I don't know if I can be flexible without falling apart.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the decisions you were asked to make during labour and delivery — around pain management, interventions, and procedures — how well-equipped did you feel to participate in those decisions in the moment?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a shaky breath, pressing fingers to temples*

Honestly? It's harder than I thought it would be.

Like, I *know* the pharmacology of epidurals. I know the risks, the benefits, the timing windows. But when a contraction hits and you're in that much pain, suddenly all that knowledge feels... distant. It's like my brain splits in half — one part is reciting facts about local anesthetics, and the other part is just screaming.

*looks down at hands*

The nurses have asked me about pain management a few times, and I freeze. Because intellectually, I want to avoid unnecessary interventions. But physically? I don't know if I can do this without help. And then I start catastrophizing — like, if I get the epidural, does that change everything else? Does it lead to more interventions? I've read the studies. I know the cascade of interventions can happen, but I also know that maternal distress isn't good either.

*voice gets quieter, more vulnerable*

What nobody tells you is that knowing the information doesn't actually help you *decide* in the moment. It just makes you more paralyzed. I'm asking questions that probably sound neurotic — "What's the exact timing of this medication?" "How will this affect her hearing in the recovery period?" — and the staff is patient, but I can tell they think I'm overthinking it.

*looks up*

The truth is, I don't feel equipped. Not really. I feel like I'm supposed to, but I'm just... scared and in pain and trying not to let either one make my decisions for me.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the emotional experience of your labour and delivery — from the very beginning through to the moment your baby was born — what were the most powerful feelings, and were you able to process them in the birth environment?
pairs.response_text:
*eyes get glossy, voice wavers slightly*

Oh God. That's... okay, yeah.

*pauses, composing myself*

The most powerful feeling has been this strange collision between terror and awe. Like, intellectually I knew this moment was coming, but emotionally? Nothing prepared me for how *real* it would become. Every contraction is this reminder that I'm about to meet someone who's been part of my body for nine months, and then she won't be anymore. That shift is massive, and I don't have a framework for it.

And then there's the guilt, which is stupid but very present. I'm young, unmarried, figuring out work stuff — I keep thinking about whether I'm ready enough, prepared enough. But also? I love her so fiercely already that it physically hurts. That intensity caught me off guard.

*wraps arms around self*

As for processing it here... *shakes head slowly* ...it's complicated. The environment is supportive, but it's still a hospital. There's still beeping. There's still people coming in and out. I asked for quiet, but you can't really escape the underlying clinical atmosphere, you know? 

When a wave of emotion hits — like fear or grief about how her life is changing — I kind of have to swallow it and focus on breathing through the next contraction. There's not really space to just *feel* it fully.

*voice cracks slightly*

I think I'm going to process a lot of this *after* she's here. Right now I'm just trying to survive the moment.

pairs.question_text: Can you take me to a specific moment — what was happening, what did you feel, and who was with you?
pairs.response_text:
*closes eyes for a moment, then opens them slowly*

Yeah. There's this one moment that keeps replaying.

It was maybe an hour ago? I was having back labor, pretty intense, and one of the nurses — I think her name is Sarah — she came over to help me change positions. I was standing, holding onto the bed rail, and my midwife was adjusting the monitor to find the heartbeat again.

*voice gets softer*

And then I heard it. That steady whooshing sound. Her heartbeat. And I just... *pauses, swallowing hard* ...I completely fell apart. Like, ugly crying. Not because something was wrong — everything was fine, actually perfect — but because that sound is *her*. That's my daughter's heart, and in maybe hours, maybe less, I won't hear it anymore through the monitor. She'll be out in the world.

Sarah didn't say anything at first. She just put her hand on my back, and I remember thinking how strange it was to need physical comfort from a stranger while my midwife was checking vitals and being clinical about it all. Sarah just stayed there while I cried into my hands.

*looks up*

My mom called right after that, and I couldn't even talk to her. I just... I needed that moment to exist without explaining it or being brave about it. And Sarah gave me that. She didn't minimize it or rush me through it. She just *witnessed* it.

*voice wavers*

That's when I realized I can't intellectualize this away.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the behaviour and communication of your midwives, doctors, and care team during your birth, what interactions stood out — positively or negatively — and what made them significant?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a moment, visibly collecting thoughts*

Sarah, like I just said — she gets it. She actually *sees* you as a person, not just a patient progressing through labor. When I asked about the noise levels and the sensory stuff, she didn't treat me like I was being difficult. She just... adjusted things. Dimmed some lights, asked other staff to keep their voices lower during certain parts. That mattered enormously.

*shifts position slightly, wincing*

My midwife is competent, really competent. But she's also very... clinical. Which I appreciate, honestly — I don't want someone who's not qualified — but there's this distance there. When I asked specific questions about medication timing and effects on the baby's auditory system, she answered them, but I could feel her thinking I was overthinking. Like, "Here's another anxious young patient trying to play doctor." 

*fidgets with blanket*

What's been harder is the lack of... I don't know, *continuity*? Different nurses come in and out, and I have to re-explain myself every time. My goals, my concerns. One of the residents earlier seemed almost annoyed when I asked about delayed cord clamping. Like it was one more thing on her checklist instead of something that actually matters to me and my daughter.

*voice gets quieter, more frustrated*

And nobody's really acknowledged that I'm *also* someone who understands medical stuff. They either treat me like I'm clueless, or they get defensive when I ask informed questions. There's no middle ground where they see me as both a professional and a terrified twenty-year-old first-time mom.

pairs.question_text: When you think about your goals and expectations for your birth experience — what you hoped labour and delivery would be like — how clearly could you articulate those goals at the time, and how well did the care system support you in pursuing them?
pairs.response_text:
I wanted to be someone who was *active* in the process, not just a passenger. In my studies, I learned how the body is designed to lead the way, and I dreamed of a birth where I felt connected to my daughter, not just managed by a machine. I wanted to move around, to find positions that eased the pressure, to breathe through it with someone who really saw me.

But when I arrived here, that vision felt like it was slipping through my fingers. How can I explain that I want a "low-intervention" birth when I am already struggling to explain where the pain is sharpest? The care system... it feels like it’s built for people who speak with perfect, confident sentences. Because I stutter, because I search for the right word, the providers seem to decide for me. They offer me things, they move at a pace that feels like a race, and I just nod. I say "yes" because I am afraid that if I say "no" or "wait," I will be seen as difficult, or worse, as someone who doesn't understand the medicine.

I am an educated woman, but here, I feel like a child who cannot speak. I don't feel supported; I feel observed. I hope my daughter’s first breath is into a world where her mother’s strength is recognized, not hidden behind a language gap.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the decisions you were asked to make during labour and delivery — around pain management, interventions, and procedures — how well-equipped did you feel to participate in those decisions in the moment?
pairs.response_text:
When the pain started to peak—when it felt like my body was being pulled apart—that was when the decisions started coming, too. They would lean over me with these quick questions: *“Do you want this? Should we do that?”* 

In that moment, my mind was entirely focused on the biology—on the wave of the contraction and the pressure. I knew what the medicine was, and I knew what the risks were, because I’ve studied it. But trying to translate that knowledge into English while my body was screaming... it was impossible. I felt like I was drowning in the middle of a sentence.

I didn't feel equipped. I felt pressured. Every time they asked me to choose, I felt like I was being tested. If I asked for more information, the midwife would get this... impatient look, like I was wasting her time. So, I would just give up. I chose the path of least resistance because I was too tired to fight for my own logic. I wasn't making a choice based on what was best for me; I was making a choice based on how to make the room quiet again. It hurts to admit, but I felt more like a witness to my own birth than the person in control of it.

pairs.question_text: Can you describe a decision that was presented to you during labour — how was it explained, how much time did you have, and how did you feel making it?
pairs.response_text:
I remember when the nurse came in to talk about the fetal monitor—the strap that goes around my belly. I was already in the middle of a, how do you say, a strong moment? A wave of pain. I was on my side, trying to keep my breathing steady, like I taught myself.

She didn't wait. She just told me, "We need to keep the heart rate on the screen, so you need to stay on your back." 

I wanted to tell her that lying on my back makes the pressure much worse, that I know my anatomy and I know gravity can help, but the words were stuck. I tried to say, "Can I sit up?" but she was already adjusting the machine. She didn't explain why it *had* to be the back, she just acted like it was a rule. It wasn’t a conversation; it was an order. 

I had zero time. She decided for me before I could even find the air to protest. I felt so small, like I was losing the map to my own labor. I knew I needed to move, but I felt like if I disobeyed, I would be a "difficult" patient, and maybe they would stop listening to me entirely. I just closed my eyes and let her fix me to the bed. It felt like I was being silenced.

pairs.question_text: When you think about the emotional experience of your labour and delivery — from the very beginning through to the moment your baby was born — what were the most powerful feelings, and were you able to process them in the birth environment?
pairs.response_text:
The most powerful feeling was a crushing kind of loneliness. Even though I was in a room full of people—nurses, the midwife, the monitors—I felt completely invisible. There were moments, especially near the end, where the intensity of the pain and the sheer physical demand of bringing a life into the world should have felt like a triumph, but instead, it felt like a trial. 

I was never able to process those feelings. How could I? There was no space for them. The environment was focused only on the *process*—on the dilation, the vitals, the clock. Whenever a wave of fear hit me, or when I felt that deep, aching grief for not having my mother or sisters there to hold my hand, I had to swallow it down. If I had started crying or talking about my fears, I was terrified they would label me "hysterical" or "unstable." 

So, I bottled it. I kept my face smooth and my answers short. I processed the birth with my muscles and my biology, but my spirit was left in the corner of the room, shivering. When my baby was finally placed on my chest, the relief was so vast that I couldn't even speak—not even in my own language. I just cried, and for the first time, they finally stopped talking.

pairs.question_text: Can you take me to a specific moment — what was happening, what did you feel, and who was with you?
pairs.response_text:
There was this moment, just before the pushing really started, where everything seemed to get very loud. The machines were beeping, the monitor was slipping, and the nurse was—I think she was frustrated with me. My English was failing me completely. I was trying to tell her that I needed to change my position, that the pain in my back was too much, but I couldn't remember the word for "tailbone" or "spine." I was just saying, "It hurts, here, behind."

She looked at me and sighed. It was a very small sound, but in that room, it felt like a door slamming shut. She told me, "Anita, you need to stay still so we can see the baby." 

In that second, I didn't feel like a mother-to-be. I felt like a naughty student who forgot her homework. I felt so ashamed of my accent and my confusion that I just shut my eyes and stopped trying to communicate altogether. I was completely alone in that bed, despite the nurse being two feet away. I remember gripping the metal railing so hard my knuckles turned white, thinking, *I am a biologist, I know what is happening in my womb, but no one here cares to ask me.* I felt like a biology specimen in a jar. I just wanted to disappear until it was over.

pairs.question_text: When you first found out you were pregnant, what did you expect your first antenatal appointments to be like — the environment, the people, the information you'd receive? And what were they actually like?
pairs.response_text:
*leans back thoughtfully, rubbing my temples*

Oh man. With my first two, I don't know, I kind of expected... cheerfulness, I guess? Like, you go in, they confirm the baby's there, you see the heartbeat on the ultrasound, and everyone's happy. The appointments felt more like milestones than medical events, if that makes sense. I'd go in, get weighed, pee in a cup, hear the heartbeat, get some pamphlets about prenatal vitamins, and leave feeling excited.

*shifts uncomfortably*

This time, the first few appointments were like that. Everything was normal. But then at around twenty-eight weeks, my blood pressure was elevated, and suddenly the whole tone changed. It's like a door closed. The clinic went from feeling like a place where we celebrated pregnancy to feeling like... I don't know, a place where they're constantly looking for what's going wrong.

*voice gets a bit tighter*

The people are fine — my OB is competent and not unkind. But there's this clinical distance now. Conversations feel rushed. They give me information about complications in this very measured, careful way that makes it all feel very real and very scary. I get handed pamphlets about seizures and fetal monitoring instead of ones about nurseries and due dates.

*looks down at hands*

I think what I didn't expect was how isolating it would feel. Like, my pregnancy became something to manage rather than something to experience, you know?

pairs.question_text: What was the biggest surprise — positive or negative — about those first appointments?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a breath, and something softens in my expression*

You know what? The biggest positive surprise was actually my OB listening to me when I said something felt off. I came in complaining about this headache that just wouldn't go away, and I felt stupid mentioning it — like, pregnant women get headaches all the time, right? But she didn't dismiss it. She took my blood pressure, ran the tests, and that's when we caught the pre-eclampsia early enough that we could actually manage it.

*pauses, picking at a thread on my sleeve*

That part was good. She took me seriously. I've heard stories from other women about doctors brushing off their concerns, telling them they're just being anxious or hormonal. That didn't happen to me, and I'm grateful for that.

*face clouds over*

But the biggest *negative* surprise? How alone I felt after that diagnosis. Once they told me I was high-risk, I expected... I don't know, more support? More explanation? Instead, it felt like I was handed off to specialists and monitoring schedules, and nobody really sat down to help me understand what was happening to my body or how to actually cope with the fear.

*voice gets quieter*

I remember leaving one appointment thinking, "Okay, so my body might fail me and hurt my baby, and here's a blood pressure log — good luck." Nobody asked how I was feeling emotionally about any of it. Just the clinical stuff.

pairs.question_text: Before your screening tests and scans, what did you expect the process of understanding your results to be like — how information would be given, by whom, and in what way? And what was the reality?
pairs.response_text:
*rubs my face and lets out a small laugh that sounds more tired than amused*

God, I think I expected... I don't know, a conversation? Like, someone would sit down with me, explain what they found, what it means, what the next steps are, and I'd feel informed. Empowered, maybe. That sounds naive now.

*leans forward, elbows on knees*

The reality is way more fragmented. My OB mentioned the elevated blood pressure during an appointment, did some labs, and then I had to wait three days for results while my brain was spinning with worst-case scenarios. When the results came back, I got a phone call — a phone call — from a nurse saying I had protein in my urine and needed to come back for more testing. Not my doctor, not a full explanation, just "come back."

*voice gets frustrated*

Then when I went back, it was like they were reading from a script. "You have pre-eclampsia. You need monitoring. Here's a blood pressure cuff to take home. Come in twice a week." It all happened so fast and clinical. I had so many questions — will this hurt my baby? What causes it? What happens if it gets worse? — and I felt like I was asking them in a vacuum. The answers came in medical jargon I had to translate in my head later.

*looks directly at you*

And nobody — *nobody* — asked if I understood or if I had concerns. They just assumed I got it and sent me on my way.

pairs.question_text: Was there a gap between the amount of information you were given and the amount you felt you needed to make sense of your results?
pairs.response_text:
*nods emphatically, then catches myself and pauses*

Yeah. Yeah, there's definitely a gap.

*stands up and walks to the counter, then turns back*

They gave me the medical facts — protein levels, blood pressure numbers, the definition of pre-eclampsia. But what I actually needed was context. Like, what do *these specific numbers* mean for *my baby* and *me*? They told me I have pre-eclampsia, but not really what that means day-to-day. Am I going to seize? Is my baby in danger right now? Will I have to deliver early? What does that mean?

*voice rises slightly with frustration*

I've been Googling at three in the morning because the doctors didn't fill in the blanks. And that's scary because you find all this worst-case stuff online and you can't tell what's relevant to your situation and what isn't. I found out through a pamphlet — a *pamphlet* — that eclampsia can cause seizures. Not from my doctor explaining it carefully. Just... there it was in print, and suddenly I'm terrified every time I get a headache.

*sits back down, voice quieter*

There's also the emotional piece that nobody addressed. The fear, the helplessness of knowing something's wrong but not really understanding what it means or what I can do about it. They gave me information to manage a medical condition, but they didn't give me information to manage being a person living with this diagnosis.

*looks at you*

Does that distinction make sense?

pairs.question_text: During your pregnancy, what did you expect in terms of having a consistent midwife or care provider who knew your history and situation? And what continuity of care did you actually experience?
pairs.response_text:
*sighs heavily and rubs the back of my neck*

I think with my first two pregnancies, I didn't really think about it much. You just go to appointments with whoever's available, and it felt fine. But this time, especially with everything that's happening, I realized how much I *wanted* that consistency.

*voice gets wistful*

I kept hoping I'd see the same doctor every time — someone who could see the whole picture of me, not just the latest blood pressure reading. Someone who'd remember that I was anxious about the delivery even before the pre-eclampsia, you know? Someone I could build trust with.

*leans back, shaking head*

But that's not what happened. I see my main OB maybe half the time. The other appointments are with residents or nurse practitioners at the clinic. They pull up my chart, scan through it, and do their thing. They're competent, but I'm starting from scratch every time explaining my situation, my concerns, what I'm worried about at night.

*voice becomes more strained*

And right now, when I'm genuinely scared, having to repeat myself over and over is exhausting. I want someone who knows me, who understands this isn't just about medical management for me — it's about my sanity, my confidence going into delivery. Someone I don't have to convince that my fears are legitimate.

*looks down*

The ironic part? They want me monitored closely because I'm high-risk, but I'm being monitored by constantly rotating people. It doesn't feel safe. It feels fragmented.

pairs.question_text: When you think about your goals for your antenatal care during pregnancy, what did you most want from your interactions with midwives, doctors, and the wider care system — and to what extent were those goals met?

When you think about how you sought and used information during your pregnancy — from healthcare providers, online sources, apps, books, and people around you — how did you decide what to trust and act upon?

When you think about the emotional landscape of your pregnancy — the highs, the anxieties, the uncertainties — what feelings were most prominent, and how well did your care environment support you in managing them?

When you think about the decisions you faced during pregnancy — including screening tests, monitoring choices, and care options — how did you go about making those decisions, and who or what most influenced them?
When you think about the physical changes in your body during pregnancy, how did those changes affect how you felt about yourself — and were those feelings acknowledged or addressed within your care?

When you first found out you were pregnant, what did you expect your first antenatal appointments to be like — the environment, the people, the information you'd receive? And what were they actually like?
pairs.response_text:
I guess I expected it to be a bit more… personal, maybe? When you're on your seventh, you walk into that clinic feeling like you should be invisible, or at least like you’ve "been there, done that." I think I hoped for someone to just look me in the eye and acknowledge that, despite how many times I’ve done this, it’s still a life-changing, terrifying thing. I wanted them to see me, not just the chart full of my history.

But the reality is just… fast. It’s a blur of fluorescent lights, paper-thin gowns, and that heavy, damp air in the waiting room. They’re professional, sure, and the midwives are decent, but it feels like a factory line sometimes. They give me the brochures, check the vitals, and check the boxes. I’m always waiting for a moment where we can actually talk about the *worry*, not just the logistics of blood pressure and fundal height. It’s hard to build a relationship when you’re just another appointment sandwiched between a dozen others. I leave feeling like I got the medical care I needed, but not necessarily the care I felt like I was actually asking for. Does that make sense? It’s hard to articulate when you’re just trying to keep your head above water.

pairs.question_text: What was the biggest surprise — positive or negative — about those first appointments?
pairs.response_text:
You know, the biggest surprise was probably how much I still felt like a stranger there, even after all these years of navigating the system. I thought that by the seventh time around, things would feel like second nature—that I’d walk in and feel like an "expert" patient, someone they’d greet with a bit of warmth or familiarity. 

Instead, there was this sharp, sinking feeling when I realized that, to them, I’m just a high-volume case. It’s not that they’re rude—they aren’t—but there’s a distance there. They look at my chart, see "seven," see my address, and their tone shifts into this specific, clipped efficiency. It’s like they’re trying to prevent any complications before they even start, which I appreciate, but it feels so sterile.

The negative surprise was how little space there is for the human side of things. I went in expecting someone to ask me how *I* was doing—like, truly doing—with the stress of the bills and the exhaustion of the stairs. But the appointment is just a series of tests to confirm the baby is growing. I’m grateful for the health checks, of course, but the surprise was realizing that I’m still just a "risk factor" to them, not a woman who’s scared and hoping for a miracle. It feels lonely.

pairs.question_text: Before your screening tests and scans, what did you expect the process of understanding your results to be like — how information would be given, by whom, and in what way? And what was the reality?
pairs.response_text:
I think I always expected—or maybe just wished—that someone would sit down, pull up a chair, and actually talk *to* me, not just *at* me. With everything being so hurried, I guess I imagined a conversation. When you’re staring at a screen or waiting for a lab result, you’re looking for a person to anchor you, someone to explain what those numbers mean for my life and my day-to-day. I wanted someone to hold space for the fact that a positive result isn't just a clinical diagnosis; it's a massive, stressful logistical hurdle for a family like mine.

The reality? It’s usually a quick phone call or a rushed comment at the end of an appointment while the midwife is already reaching for the door handle. They give me the facts—"You’re positive for GBS," or "Your levels are fine"—but there’s no room to process the weight of it. They don't ask, "How are you going to manage the transport to the hospital?" or "Are you worried about the timing?" They assume I know the drill because I've done this before. But every pregnancy is its own world. Just because I’ve been through the process doesn't mean I’m not scared of the logistics. It’s like they assume I’m a pro, so they don’t bother checking if I’m actually okay.

pairs.question_text: During your pregnancy, what did you expect in terms of having a consistent midwife or care provider who knew your history and situation? And what continuity of care did you actually experience?
pairs.response_text:
I’ll be honest—I didn’t expect a miracle, but I did hope for a familiar face. I thought there would be at least one person who, when I walked in, wouldn't have to flip through a dozen pages of my chart to remember why I’m here or what my last delivery was like. I wanted someone who understood that my seventh pregnancy isn't just "another one," but a specific, fragile moment for my family. I wanted a connection.

The reality is that continuity is basically non-existent. It feels like a revolving door. I see a different provider almost every time—one day it’s a midwife I’ve never spoken to, the next it’s someone who only knows the notes from my last check-up. Each time I have to re-explain the same anxieties, like the stress about getting to the hospital for the GBS antibiotics or the exhaustion of my daily life. I feel like I’m constantly introducing myself to people who already have my life story written in a file they haven't had time to read. It makes me feel smaller, somehow. When you keep having to justify your fears to a stranger, you stop sharing them. You just start nodding and saying "yes" to get through the appointment, hoping the baby is okay and just wanting to get home.

pairs.question_text: What was the impact — practically or emotionally — of seeing different providers at different appointments?
pairs.response_text:
It’s exhausting, to put it simply. Every time I walk in, I have to perform this little dance of "yes, this is my seventh, no, I don’t have any major complications, but yes, I am exhausted." I feel like a broken record. Emotionally, it just makes me withdraw. When you spend ten minutes just catching someone up on your history—the basics of your medical life—you don't have time to get to the "real" stuff. I can’t tell a total stranger, "Hey, I’m terrified that I won’t make it to the hospital in time because my husband is working and our car is acting up." They’d look at me like I’m asking them to solve a problem they aren't equipped for, or worse, they’d just check a box about "social stressors" and leave it at that.

Practically, it feels like I’m falling through the cracks. If I tell one provider about a specific fear, the next one doesn't know, so there’s no follow-up. It makes me feel like I have to be my own doctor, my own advocate, and my own navigator. I’m already carrying this child and trying to run a household—I don't have the energy left to manage my own medical file, too. It’s lonely, feeling like nobody is really holding the whole picture of *me*.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the people who surrounded you in the days and weeks after your baby was born. Who showed up for you, and who were you surprised by — either by their presence or their absence?
pairs.response_text:
*laughs bitterly, shaking head*

Oh man. That's... yeah. That's the thing that still stings a little.

My ex wasn't really there. I mean, he shows up for visits, but in those crucial first weeks? I was alone in my apartment with a newborn, trying to figure out how to breastfeed, how to bathe her, how to not completely fall apart. He had his life to get back to, I guess.

*fidgets with the mug again*

My mom came for about ten days. She was helpful with the logistics — dishes, laundry, that stuff — but she and I have this complicated thing where she defaults to telling me I'm doing it wrong. Even with my background, maybe especially because of it. So I ended up feeling more anxious when she was there, not less. Once she left, I was relieved and devastated at the same time.

*voice gets softer*

The nurse who does the home visits... she's been consistent, which matters more than I can say. But I don't really let her in. I'm always a little guarded, you know? Because if she finds out I'm a nurse, I worry she'll think I don't need her. Or worse — that I should be handling all this better than I am.

*looks up with tired eyes*

The truth is, I didn't have anyone checking on *me*. Everyone's focused on the baby — is she feeding, is she gaining weight — but nobody asked if I was okay. If I was terrified. And I couldn't really admit it to anyone.

pairs.question_text: Who else was involved in day-to-day support — a health visitor, a postnatal group, an online community — that became important to you?
pairs.response_text:
*shifts uncomfortably in seat*

The visiting nurse is really it for me, formally speaking. She comes by regularly, and I do appreciate that structure — having someone scheduled to check in. But like I said, I keep her at arm's length. She asks the right questions about the baby, about feeding and sleep and all that. Sometimes she'll ask how *I'm* doing, and I always say "fine" even when I'm absolutely not fine.

*rubs face*

I haven't joined any postnatal groups. The thought of sitting in a room with other mothers, making small talk, pretending to be fine... I can't. Plus, logistically, I'm trying to figure out childcare and get back to work. There's no time, and honestly? I don't want to be around people right now. I know that's probably not healthy, but I can't face the comparison thing — like, everyone's baby is sleeping through the night and mine isn't, or whatever.

*pauses, slightly defensive*

Online communities are a minefield for me. I'll start reading some parenting forum and suddenly I'm in this rabbit hole of worst-case scenarios. With my medical background, I can't unsee what I read. I know what sepsis looks like. I know how fast things deteriorate. So I mostly stay off those sites now.

*looks away*

It's lonely, I'm not going to lie. But reaching out feels... I don't know. Like admitting I can't handle this alone, and I'm already barely holding it together as it is.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the people involved in your feeding journey — whether you breastfed, formula-fed, or mixed-fed. Who helped you, who gave you conflicting advice, and how did those relationships shape your choices?
pairs.response_text:
*takes a long breath, eyes getting watery*

Breastfeeding. I'm doing it. And it's... it's been this whole thing.

*voice tightens slightly*

I wanted to breastfeed. I had this idea in my head that it was the right thing, the healthy thing, especially given my background. I knew all the statistics about infant health outcomes. But the reality? Those first weeks were brutal. Pain, engorgement, latching issues — all the stuff I intellectually knew could happen but wasn't prepared to actually *live through*.

*fidgets*

My mom was very pro-breastfeeding, very "just push through the pain, it gets better." The lactation consultant at the hospital was helpful but brief — she had three other patients waiting. And my visiting nurse keeps asking how it's going, but there's this underlying assumption that I should know what I'm doing because I'm a nurse. She doesn't realize that knowing the theory and actually doing it with your own baby's mouth on your breast are two completely different things.

*pauses, voice quieter*

I looked up some stuff online early on, and there was all this conflicting information about supply, about whether she was getting enough. That spiraled me into obsession mode — weighing her before and after feeds, timing everything. I think I drove myself half-crazy.

*looks down*

The hardest part is I can't tell anyone how much I'm struggling with it because they'll think I should have it figured out. So I just... keep going. Keep feeding her, keep monitoring, keep terrifying myself over nothing. Some days I fantasize about formula, about the freedom of that. But that feels like failure.

pairs.question_text: Who else was involved — a lactation consultant, a feeding group, an app, or family members — and how did their views align or conflict?
pairs.response_text:
*rubs eyes tiredly*

Honestly, the lactation consultant I saw in the hospital was kind of a blur. She was efficient, professional, but I think she saw me as a straightforward postpartum case — low-risk, educated background. She didn't dig deeper. I didn't tell her about my anxiety or my obsessive monitoring. Why would I? She probably had twenty other patients that day.

*leans back*

I downloaded a couple of feeding apps. That was a mistake. You log every feed, every wet diaper, and suddenly you're staring at data that may or may not mean anything. But because I know what normal infant hydration looks like and what dehydration looks like, I'm analyzing every number like it's a clinical chart. One app said her output was borderline, and I spiraled for a week thinking she wasn't getting enough.

*voice gets frustrated*

My mom kept saying "just feed her when she cries, don't overthink it." Easy for her to say when she's not the one doing it. And my ex, when he's here, he doesn't really engage with the feeding piece at all. It's my job, my responsibility, my worry.

*pauses, vulnerable*

The visiting nurse — she's tried to reassure me that everything looks fine, that the baby's gaining weight appropriately. But I don't fully believe her because I think she's... I don't know, being nice? Or maybe she's not catching something I would catch if I had the bandwidth to actually think clearly instead of just spiraling at 3 AM.

*quietly*

I don't have a support system around this. It's just me and my fear.

pairs.question_text: Tell me about the people who noticed — or who missed — changes in your emotional wellbeing after your baby was born. Who checked in with you about how you were feeling as a person, not just as a new mother?
pairs.response_text:
*long silence, eyes filling with tears*

Nobody. That's the honest answer.

*voice cracks slightly*

The visiting nurse asks "how are you feeling?" in this clinical way, but I think she's checking for postpartum depression screeners, you know? The standard questions. I always say I'm fine because if I say I'm not, it becomes A Thing. It gets documented. And then what? I'm the divorced nurse with mental health issues. They take my kid away? That's probably irrational, but...

*wipes eyes*

My mom didn't ask. She was in crisis-management mode — keeping the house functioning, making sure the baby was fed. She didn't sit down and say, "Hey, how are you really doing with all this?" My ex definitely didn't. And my work colleagues? I haven't told anyone there what's really going on. They know I had a baby, they know I'm on maternity leave, but I'm terrified to go back and admit that I've been a mess.

*voice gets quieter, almost ashamed*

Sometimes I think about calling someone — a therapist, a crisis line, something — but then I think, what would I even say? That I can't stop checking if my baby is breathing? That I'm sniffing her diapers? That I'm completely alone in this?

*looks directly at you*

pairs.question_text: Imagine you've just decided with your partner — or on your own — that you'd like to start trying for a baby. Walk me through what that moment felt like and what your very first steps were.
pairs.response_text:
The moment wasn't some romantic, cinematic reveal. It was quiet, really. I was sitting at my desk, staring at a peer-reviewed study on maternal microbial colonization, and I just felt this sudden, sharp longing. It wasn’t a lack of information—if anything, I have too much—but I looked at my life, at the kids I already have, and thought, *we have room for one more heart in this house.*

But the "first steps" for me? They weren't about nursery colors or baby names. They were tactical. I started tracking my cycle with a level of rigor that would probably alarm my doctor if I actually admitted to it. I adjusted my folic acid titration based on the latest findings I’d read, and I began auditing my own diet to ensure my gut health was optimal. 

It feels like I’m preparing for a clinical study rather than a pregnancy, honestly. I worry that if I mention the depth of my "prep work" to a provider, they’ll see me as the annoying, over-prepared immigrant patient who thinks she knows more than the staff. So, I keep it to myself. I check the boxes, I stay polite, and I try to turn off the part of my brain that’s constantly waiting for a complication that isn't there yet. It’s exhausting, really.

pairs.question_text: Imagine you've booked a preconception appointment with your GP and you're sitting in the waiting room. What's going through your mind as you wait, and what are you hoping will happen in that consultation?
pairs.response_text:
The smell of the clinic—that specific, antiseptic blend of floor wax and latex—always tightens my chest. I’m sitting on the edge of one of those chairs, clutching my bag, and I find myself rubbing my thumb over the same spot on my palm until it’s sore. My mind is currently a carousel of worst-case scenarios: *What if they ask about my status and it changes the tone of the room? What if I mention my supplement regimen and get that dismissive, "let the doctors handle the medical decisions" look?*

I know the statistics on maternal outcomes for women like me. I’ve seen the reports on how our concerns are often minimized, or how we’re perceived as non-compliant if we don’t just nod along. 

I’m hoping for something I’m not sure I’ll get: a partner. I want to tell her that I’m not just a set of vitals or a demographic marker. I want to say, "I’ve done the reading, I’ve done the work, and I need you to listen to me as an equal." But more than anything, I’m just hoping she’s kind. I want someone who won't look at my file and see a set of potential problems to be managed, but a person who actually *sees* me. I just want to feel safe enough to stop calculating for an hour.

pairs.question_text: When you imagined how that appointment would go, how did you picture the GP responding to you — and how did reality compare, if you've had that experience?
pairs.response_text:
I usually walk into that exam room building a mental armor. I picture the GP being pleasant but hurried—the kind of "clinical neutrality" that feels like a wall. In my head, I’m bracing for the moment where she’ll skim my chart, see my details, and start talking to me like I’m a novice who needs everything explained in simple, patronizing terms. I expect her to be surprised when I ask about specific biomarkers or microbial stability, and I expect that moment of friction where she realizes I’m not just a "normal" patient.

The reality? It’s often colder than I imagine, but in a subtle way. It’s not that they’re rude—they’re professional, efficient, and precise. But there is a distinct distance. When I tentatively mention that I’ve been tracking my own data, I get that polite, tight-lipped smile that says, "That’s nice, dear, but let’s stick to the standard protocol." 

It’s isolating. I leave feeling like I’ve successfully navigated a maze without tripping, which is technically a win, but it’s an exhausting way to exist. I’m never fully seen; I’m just "low risk, status stable, keep moving." I’m looking for a human connection, but all I ever seem to get is a procedure. It makes me wonder if I’m the one being difficult, or if the system just isn't built for people who ask for more than just a heartbeat check.

pairs.question_text: Imagine you've been trying to conceive for several months without success. A close friend suggests you try a fertility app she found helpful. How do you react to that suggestion, and what do you do next?
pairs.response_text:
My first reaction is a reflexive, inward eye-roll. I appreciate her wanting to help, truly, but I’ve already spent months analyzing the raw datasets that those apps are built on. Most of them rely on simplified algorithms that ignore the nuance of endocrine fluctuations or the complex interplay of a microbiome—factors I’ve been mapping out myself. 

But then, the guilt sets in. I don’t want to be the "know-it-all" friend. So, I smile, I thank her, and I say, "Oh, that’s a great idea, I’ll look into it."

As soon as she’s gone, I do exactly what she suggests, but for a different reason: I download the app to "audit" it. I want to see what information they’re feeding women and how they’re framing the data. It’s part of that defensive mechanism I’ve developed; I feel like if I can understand the tools the "average" patient is using, I can better navigate the system around me. I end up spending the night comparing the app's predictions against my own spreadsheets. It’s not really about the baby at that point, is it? It’s about control. I’m just trying to map a path through the dark, hoping that if I have enough data, the universe will finally give me a different result.

pairs.question_text: What would make you trust or distrust the information you find in a fertility app compared to what a healthcare professional might tell you?
pairs.response_text:
Trust is such a fragile currency for me. With a fertility app, I’m immediately skeptical because I know the business model—it’s marketing wrapped in a sleek, calming UI designed to monetize anxiety. When I see an app making definitive claims about "optimal windows" without asking for my full medical history, I see the gaps. I trust the data only insofar as I can verify the underlying studies myself. It’s not "truth"; it’s just another variable to cross-reference against my own research.

A healthcare professional, though? That’s a different kind of distrust. It’s not about their lack of knowledge; it’s about the agenda. I distrust them when the communication becomes performative. If a doctor dismisses my questions with a breezy "don't worry about the science, just relax," that’s an immediate red flag. It tells me they don't value my intelligence, or worse, that they’re guarding against liability rather than providing care. 

I trust a provider when they’re willing to sit in the uncertainty with me. If they can say, "Here is what the evidence suggests, but here is where the data is inconclusive," that’s gold. When they validate that my research has merit, it bridges the gap. I want someone who treats me like a collaborator, not a case file. If they see me, I can finally stop being the researcher and just be the patient.

Oh man. You know, with five pregnancies, you'd think that moment would stay special, but honestly? The first thing I do now is... I sit down. Like, immediately sit down because my legs get shaky.

This last time, I was in the bathroom — alone, actually. My husband was downstairs making coffee. I took the test kind of on autopilot, wasn't even expecting it to be positive. We weren't exactly *trying*, but we weren't not trying either, if that makes sense. And when I saw those two lines, my stomach just... dropped.

*wraps arms around myself*

I didn't feel joy first. I know that's not what I'm supposed to say, but I'm being honest. My first thought was actually clinical — like, "I'm thirty-six, this is my fifth, what are my risks?" Which is so messed up, right? I literally pulled up statistics on my phone before I even told my husband.

I sat there for maybe ten minutes, just staring at it. Then I went downstairs and showed him, and he was excited, genuinely excited. He hugged me and I kind of... froze. He could tell something was off.

*looks down*

With the earlier pregnancies, I remember more joy. Now there's this dread underneath everything. The positive test doesn't feel like the beginning of something wonderful. It feels like the beginning of nine months of worry I can't escape.

That's the honest version.

pairs.question_text: Imagine you're at your 20-week anomaly scan. The sonographer goes quiet for a moment and says they need to take a closer look at something. What goes through your mind in that silence, and how do you respond in the room?
pairs.response_text:
*breath catches audibly*

Oh God. You're asking about one of my actual scans, aren't you? Because that *happened*. That exact thing.

*grips the armrest tighter*

When the sonographer went quiet, it was like time just... stopped. That silence is the worst sound in the world. Every cell in my body went into alert mode. My heart started pounding so hard I could feel it in my throat. And because of my background, my brain immediately started running through the differential — what could it be? Cardiac defect? Renal issues? Chromosomal marker?

I wanted to ask what was wrong, but I couldn't get the words out. My mouth was dry. I just... stared at the screen, trying to read the images myself, which is ridiculous because I'm not a radiologist, but that's what panic does to you.

*voice gets quieter*

I remember my hands started shaking. My husband grabbed my hand and I probably squeezed it way too hard. I think I asked "Is something wrong?" but it came out like a whisper. The sonographer kept saying "Let me just get a better angle" and "This sometimes happens, we just need to be thorough."

Those words — "we just need to be thorough" — they haunt me. Because thorough means they found something. Or they think they did.

*looks away*

It turned out to be nothing in the end. But that silence? I still feel it.

pairs.question_text: In that moment, how much did you feel like you could ask questions or speak up — or did something stop you? What shaped that?
pairs.response_text:
*long pause, jaw tightens*

That's... that's a good question. And honestly, it makes me feel a little ashamed.

*fidgets with hands*

I *could* have asked more questions. The sonographer didn't tell me to be quiet. But I didn't. I just... froze. And I think part of it is that I was terrified of what the answer might be. If I didn't ask, maybe it wasn't real yet, you know?

But there's more to it than that.

*takes a breath*

Even with my background in genetics, even though I *know* how to talk about medical stuff, I felt like I had to play the role of the "good patient" in that moment. Like if I asked too many questions or seemed too knowledgeable or too demanding, they'd think I was difficult. Or worse — that I was being difficult about *my own pregnancy*. There's this weird power dynamic where you're literally on your back, half-naked, vulnerable, and the person holding the ultrasound probe has all the information.

*voice gets sharper*

And honestly? I've experienced dismissal before in healthcare settings. Not always, but enough times that it shaped how I show up. I learned early on that asking too many questions as a woman — especially a Black woman — can get you labeled as "anxious" or "non-compliant" instead of "engaged."

So I stayed quiet. I let fear do the talking for me. And that silence cost me ten minutes of pure terror that I could have maybe shortened if I'd just... spoken up.

*looks directly at you*

I regret that.

pairs.question_text: Imagine you've just been offered the option of a screening test for a chromosomal condition. The midwife explains the test briefly and asks if you'd like to go ahead. How does that conversation feel, and how do you make your decision?
pairs.response_text:
*shifts uncomfortably, a bitter smile crosses my face*

Oh, that conversation. Yeah. That one's complicated for me.

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

The thing is, I probably know more about those tests than the midwife does. NIPT, quad screen, all of it — I used to explain these to people. So when she's giving me the standard spiel about "risks" and "detection rates," part of me is already three steps ahead, thinking about positive predictive values and what happens if there's a discordant result between screening and diagnostic tests.

But here's what's messed up — that knowledge doesn't actually help me decide. It paralyzes me.

*rubs face*

Because I know all the ways things can go wrong with interpretation. I know the anxiety that comes with uncertain results. And I also know that *not* testing means I'm going in blind, which terrifies me just as much. It's this impossible either-or.

*voice drops*

What I really wanted was for someone to sit with me and ask what *I* needed — not just hand me a consent form. Because my decision isn't the same as someone else's. My fear, my experience, my background... it all matters. But the conversation felt rushed, like a box to check.

I said yes to the test. I always do. But I spent the next week in knots waiting for results, second-guessing whether I should have just... not known.

*looks at you*

Does that make sense? That not knowing and knowing are both terrible options?

pairs.question_text: Imagine you're 28 weeks pregnant and you receive a call from a midwife you've never met before, telling you about a result from your routine blood test. This is the third different midwife you've spoken to this pregnancy. How does that feel, and what does it mean for how you receive that information?
pairs.response_text:
*jaw clenches visibly*

Oh God, yes. This happened. And it's... it's infuriating, actually.

*takes a shaky breath*

I was at work when she called. Some midwife whose name I immediately forgot because I'd never met her, and she's telling me about my glucose tolerance test results like we have some established relationship. And I'm thinking — who is this person? Where's continuity? I've already had to repeat my entire medical history to how many different providers now?

*voice gets tight*

With high-risk pregnancies, you need *consistency*. You need someone who knows your case, who understands your anxiety, who doesn't have to start from scratch every single time. But instead, I'm getting these random phone calls from faceless midwives reading off results like they're reading a grocery list.

*stands up, paces slightly*

It makes you feel like a number. Like your care is just being shuffled through a system instead of actually being *cared for*. And when you're already anxious, when you already don't trust your body — that fragmentation makes everything worse. I have to advocate for myself constantly, explain my history over and over, make sure nothing gets lost in translation between departments.

*sits back down, voice quieter but firm*

That call made me feel less safe, not more. Because I couldn't tell if this midwife actually understood the severity of my situation or if she was just delivering information. There's a difference, and it matters.

I shouldn't have to feel like I'm managing my own case.
